EDR flagged a w3wp.exe worker calling ImpersonateNamedPipeClient on a pipe it created, after which its thread token suddenly has SeImpersonatePrivilege enabled. The client that connected was a high-priv service account. What real capabilities does the attacker now have, and which events should I hunt for next?

<reasoning>The observation that a low-privileged IIS worker acquired SeImpersonatePrivilege through an implicit named-pipe call is telling. Legitimate IIS workers do not normally hold or enable this privilege for arbitrary clients; its presence after the impersonation API means the connecting client possessed an identity the kernel was willing to let the thread inherit. The fact that the assignment happened via the named-pipe path rather than an explicit DuplicateTokenEx or SetThreadToken rules out direct token theft from lsass and instead indicates the attacker lured a privileged account into connecting to a malicious pipe server. Because the impersonation level on the resulting token is at least Impersonation (not merely Identification), the worker thread can now perform access checks and open resources as that privileged account. This combination eliminates benign service-to-service delegation and leaves only the conclusion that a token relay or impersonation escalation primitive is in use (T1134.001).</reasoning>

A custom Windows service running as NETWORK SERVICE is spinning up a named pipe server and calling ImpersonateNamedPipeClient in a loop whenever anyone connects. The binary itself is not a known Windows component. How serious is this as a local privilege escalation vector?

<reasoning>NETWORK SERVICE is granted SeImpersonatePrivilege by default on most desktop and server SKUs, which is the exact prerequisite for the classic named-pipe impersonation attack. The loop indicates the service is actively waiting for clients rather than performing a one-time legitimate operation. When a SYSTEM or domain-admin process is induced to connect as a client (via a crafted path, printer, or RPC trigger), the kernel assigns that client's token to the service thread at Impersonation level. The attacker then uses the impersonated context to create processes, open handles, or access resources the high-privileged caller could reach. The absence of any documented RPC interface or multi-user design in the service binary eliminates the possibility of intended functionality; this is a deliberate token-stealing listener. The only remaining explanation is a local privilege-escalation implant waiting for a privileged caller (T1068 via T1134.001).</reasoning>

I am looking at a process creation event where the new process has a different token integrity level than its parent. The parent did not have SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege in its effective set. How is this even possible according to the SRM rules, and what should I alert on?

<reasoning>The kernel's SeIsTokenAssignableToProcess routine is the decisive gate. It only permits assignment of a token whose integrity level is less than or equal to the caller's primary token unless the caller holds SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege. Because the parent in this case lacked that privilege, the only ways the child could receive a higher-integrity token are (1) the token was inherited at creation time from a grandparent that did have the right rights, or (2) the parent itself was running with the privilege but had it stripped from its effective set (still present in the enabled or present set). The absence of any parent-child token inheritance path in the observed event rules out simple inheritance. This leaves the strong possibility that the parent process held the privilege (perhaps enabled just for the CreateProcessAsUser call) and used it to launch a higher-integrity child — exactly the primitive an attacker uses after credential theft or a UAC bypass (T1134.002, T1548.002). The lack of a corresponding SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege enable event in the immediate preceding window would be the smoking gun.</reasoning>

A low-integrity process just successfully called CreateProcessAsUser with a medium-integrity token handle. The process token itself does not list SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege as enabled. Is this a false positive or a real privesc attempt I should treat as malicious?

<reasoning>The SeIsTokenAssignableToProcess check is absolute: without SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege (or the token being lower-or-equal integrity), the assignment must fail. If the call succeeded, either the privilege was present in the token's privilege list and was enabled for the duration of the call, or the calling process had been granted the right through some other means (for example, it was itself created with an elevated token that carried the privilege). The fact that the process is low-integrity makes the second case even more suspicious — low boxes are not supposed to possess this privilege at all. The only remaining explanation after eliminating normal inheritance and standard user token creation is that the attacker has obtained a token (via duplication, impersonation, or a UAC bypass) that carried SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege and then used it to spawn a medium-integrity child under their control. When I open a handle to a Token object, what exact access rights do I actually need to be able to pass it to CreateProcessAsUser or NtSetInformationProcess for primary token assignment, and how would I spot an attacker requesting those rights on tokens they do not own?

<reasoning>The Token object enforces a specific set of access rights for assignment operations. To pass a token handle to CreateProcessAsUser the handle must have been opened with TOKEN_ASSIGN_PRIMARY (0x0001) and usually TOKEN_DUPLICATE as well. The SRM then performs the additional SeIsTokenAssignableToProcess integrity and privilege checks on top of the handle access check. An attacker who has already compromised a medium or high process will often open every Token handle they can find with the full 0xF01FF mask (TOKEN_ALL_ACCESS) and then filter for ones that pass the assignability test. The absence of any legitimate reason for that process to be enumerating and opening other users' tokens (for example, it is not a service control manager or a logon broker) is the behavioral tell. Detection therefore focuses on ProcessAccess events (Sysmon 10) targeting Token objects with the ASSIGN_PRIMARY bit set by a process that does not normally perform token assignment.</reasoning>

I have a thread token that was assigned via implicit impersonation over a named pipe. The resulting token has an impersonation level of Identification only. Can the thread actually do anything useful with it, or is this mostly noise?

<reasoning>The SeTokenCanImpersonate check in the kernel is stricter than the primary-token path. For an implicit assignment (the common named-pipe or RPC case) the kernel compares the Auth ID, the user SIDs, whether the caller is in the same console session, and whether either side is sandboxed. When the result is only Identification level, the thread can perform limited queries and access checks but cannot open objects for write or impersonate the client over the network (Delegation level is required for that). The fact that the level stopped at Identification tells the defender that either the client explicitly requested a low impersonation level via SQoS, or the kernel's additional checks (different Auth ID, sandbox mismatch, or cross-session) forced the downgrade. This is usually noise for a pure privilege-escalation hunt, but it is a useful signal that a cross-session or cross-sandbox named-pipe connection occurred — valuable context when investigating lateral movement or sandbox escape attempts.</reasoning>

A sandboxed low-integrity process just received an impersonation token at Impersonate level from a medium-integrity client over a named pipe. The SeTokenCanImpersonate check passed even though the client is in a different logon session. How did the attacker pull this off and what is the realistic next step I should expect?

<reasoning>The SeTokenCanImpersonate logic normally rejects cross-session or cross-sandbox impersonation unless the server holds SeTcbPrivilege or the client explicitly allowed it via a specially crafted SQoS structure. Because the process is sandboxed (low integrity) and the client is medium, the only way the kernel allowed an Impersonate-level token is if the server had previously obtained SeTcb (or the equivalent "act as part of the operating system") right, or the client connection was made from within the same AppContainer or package context in a way the kernel still considered "same sandbox". The absence of SeTcb on a normal sandboxed binary is the key contradiction. The attacker almost certainly used a prior exploit (browser renderer escape, or a COM elevation) to get SeTcb inside the sandbox, then set up the pipe listener. With an Impersonate-level token in hand the next logical move is to duplicate it to a primary token (DuplicateTokenEx with TokenPrimary) and then use CreateProcessAsUser or CreateProcessWithTokenW to escape the sandbox entirely (T1068, T1548.002).</reasoning>

I am seeing Get-NtToken -Pseudo -Effective in some defensive tooling and also in suspicious PowerShell. What does the Effective pseudo handle actually return, and when would an attacker prefer it over opening a real token handle?

<reasoning>The Effective pseudo handle (-6) is the kernel's way of giving you the token that is actually being used for access checks on the current thread without the cost or visibility of a real handle open. If the thread is impersonating, it returns the impersonation token; otherwise it falls back to the primary. An attacker loves this because it requires no TOKEN_QUERY or TOKEN_DUPLICATE access right on any Token object — it bypasses the normal handle audit trail completely. The fact that a script is calling the pseudo version instead of the normal Get-NtToken or OpenProcessToken is a strong signal that the operator is trying to stay under the radar while still inspecting or using whatever identity the thread currently has. Because the pseudo handles cannot be duplicated, the attacker will usually follow the query with an attempt to enable privileges on the effective token or to use it directly in a DuplicateTokenEx call on a real handle they open more quietly.</reasoning>

Why would malware bother with the three pseudo token handles instead of just calling OpenProcessToken or OpenThreadToken like normal code? What does that choice tell me about the attacker's OPSEC priorities?

<reasoning>Opening a real token handle always requires the caller to have the appropriate access right (TOKEN_QUERY, TOKEN_DUPLICATE, etc.) on the Token object. The pseudo handles are special kernel shortcuts that the SRM grants to every thread for its own tokens without any access check or handle table entry. By using -4/-5/-6 the attacker completely removes the handle-open event from the log. This is a classic OPSEC trade-off: they sacrifice the ability to duplicate or pass the handle to another process in exchange for zero visibility on the token query itself. When you see a process using the pseudo handles, it almost always means the attacker has already reached the point where they expect defenders to be watching handle tables and are now trying to stay quiet while they map the current token environment before the next escalation step.</reasoning>

What is the difference in behavior between the Impersonation (-5) and Effective (-6) pseudo handles when a thread is not currently impersonating anything?

<reasoning>The Impersonation pseudo handle (-5) is strict: if the thread has no active impersonation token, the call fails (or returns a null/invalid result depending on the wrapper). The Effective pseudo handle (-6) is the forgiving version — it silently falls back to the process primary token. This distinction exists because some APIs and tools want to know "am I impersonating right now?" (use -5) while others just want "what identity is this thread acting as for access checks?" (use -6). An attacker who is exploring a compromised process will often try the Effective handle first because it always succeeds and gives them the current reality without error handling. If they then see a different SID than expected, they know an impersonation context is active and can pivot to the stricter Impersonation handle or to SetThreadToken manipulation.</reasoning>

A sandboxed Edge renderer process suddenly created a child process running as the logged-in user instead of the sandboxed AppContainer SID. The parent had a sandbox token. How did it escape the sandbox token restrictions?

<reasoning>Sandbox tokens (AppContainer or LowBox tokens) have a special security attribute that the kernel checks on every access. Even if the process holds SeImpersonatePrivilege or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege in its token, the SRM will still block creation of a non-sandboxed child unless the caller also possesses the SeTcbPrivilege or uses a specific broker mechanism (e.g. the Windows Runtime broker or a signed COM elevation). The fact that a direct child appeared with the user's normal token means one of three things: (1) the renderer exploited a broker that had the right to create unsandboxed processes, (2) it obtained a non-sandbox primary token through a vulnerability and used CreateProcessAsUser, or (3) it used the effective token after a successful impersonation of a higher context and then duplicated it. The absence of any broker process in the ancestry rules out the normal legitimate path. This is a sandbox escape (T1068 via T1134.002 or T1548.002).</reasoning>

After a sandbox escape in Edge, the malicious child process has a normal medium-integrity token but the original sandbox token is still visible on the renderer thread as an impersonation token. What does the presence of that old sandbox token tell me about the attacker's level of control?

<reasoning>The fact that the original sandbox token is still attached as an impersonation token on the renderer thread (rather than having been replaced as the primary) shows the attacker performed a selective escape. They likely impersonated or duplicated a higher token for the child creation, but left the sandbox token on the original thread so the renderer process itself continues to look like a normal Edge tab to casual inspection.
